q: In traditional Filipino vernacular architecture, the bahay kubo is often accompanied by a separate elevated structure used specifically for storing harvested rice, grains, and food supplies. This structure protects the harvest from moisture, pests, and ground animals. What is this traditional storage structure called?
n: The kamalig is the separate raised granary for rice and food supplies. Source: Lico, Arkitekturang Filipino (2008); Klassen, Architecture in the Philippines (1986).

q: The early 20th-century public school buildings known as Gabaldon schools were funded through the 1907 law authored by Assemblyman Isauro Gabaldon, whose name became permanently associated with the standardized school prototypes designed under William E. Parsons' "tropical hybrid" philosophy. One of their most recognizable features is the building's elevation of approximately 1.20 meters above grade. What was the primary architectural purpose of this elevated platform?
o: To create a formal civic plinth that visually emphasized the school's institutional importance
To allow the underside to be enclosed later for additional instructional spaces as enrollment increased
To protect the building from flooding, enhance passive ventilation, and serve as a sanitary barrier
To provide an underfloor service zone intended for storage and maintenance access
n: Raising Gabaldon schools about 1.20 m protected them from floods, improved ventilation and acted as a sanitary barrier. Source: NHCP / DepEd, Gabaldon School Buildings (RA 11194).

q: Several major Philippine real estate developers publicly promote sustainability through green-building certifications, estate-wide environmental programs, and energy-efficient design standards. However, only one developer holds the distinction of having a residential and commercial portfolio in which every single project is certified sustainable by recognized local and global organizations such as LEED, BERDE, WELL, and EDGE—not just selected flagship developments. Which developer meets this criterion?
n: Arthaland is the developer whose entire portfolio is certified sustainable (LEED, BERDE, WELL, EDGE). Source: Arthaland Corporation sustainability reports.

q: Arthaland's flagship development, the Arthaland Century Pacific Tower in Bonifacio Global City, is internationally recognized for its LEED Platinum, BERDE 5-Star, anc EDGE Zero Carbon certifications. The tower's design was led by a globally renowned architectural firrn known for major skyscrapers such as One World Trace Center in New York. Which firm served as the lead architect for this iconic Arthaiang project?
n: Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM), architects of One World Trade Center, led the design of the Arthaland Century Pacific Tower. Source: SOM project profile, Arthaland Century Pacific Tower.

q: The Arthaland Century Pacific Tower (Act} in Bonifacio Global City is one of the Philippines' most awarded sustainable office developments, carrying LEED Platinum and BERDE 5-Star certifications as well as being the world's first EDGE Zero Carbon certified building. It is also on track for WELL v2 certification. While the conceptual design was led by an international firm, the project required a Philippine-based architectural practice to serve as the local architect of record, ensuring full compliance with national! codes, local regulations, and on-site coordination. Which major Philippine architectural firm fulfilled this role?
n: GF & Partners Architects was the local architect of record for the Arthaland Century Pacific Tower. Source: Arthaland / GF & Partners project records.

q: The Arthaland Century Pacific Tower (ACPT) uses a facade system engineered to optimize solar control, shading, and energy performance in a tropical climate. The design also conceals the podium levels while maintaining a dynamic exterior expression. Which facade strategy was actually implemented for the tower?
o: A hybrid facade combining perforated aluminum screens and vertical terracotta fins to reduce heat gain on sun-exposed elevations
A uniquely detailed system of overlapping glass panels providing orientation-based shading and concealing the podium while enhancing solar control
A full double-skin curtain wall with ventilated cavities designed to create a continuous thermal buffer around the tower
A unitized curtain wall system with deep horizontal light shelves engineered to redirect daylight into interior workspaces
n: ACPT's facade uses overlapping glass panels detailed by orientation. They shade the building, hide the podium and improve solar control. Source: SOM project profile, Arthaland Century Pacific Tower.

q: Arthaland developed a major large-scale commercial tower in Cebu IT Park designed by GF & Partners Architects, intended primarily for premium-grade office use. The project is recognized as ane of the most advanced sustainable buildings in the Philippines, having earned EDGE Zero Carbon, EDGE Advanced, LEED Gold (Core & Shell), anc BERDE 5-Star certifications. It features a high-efficiency facade, low-energy MEPF systems, and forms part of Arthaland's 100% certified sustainable portfolio, Which project fits this description?
n: Cebu Exchange Tower in Cebu IT Park, by GF & Partners, carries EDGE Zero Carbon, LEED Gold and BERDE 5-Star ratings. Source: Arthaland Corporation project records.

q: When working on heritage conservation or retrofitting of historic structures, architects and engineers often face the difficulty of integrating modern building requirements into old fabric without compromising authenticity. Which of the following represents one of the most critical challenges in such projects?
o: Lack of skilled traditional craftsmen and artisans
Transforming the structure for commercial use
Ensuring that new architectural elements visually match the original style
Integrating modern MEPFS systems into old structures without damaging historic fabric
n: A critical challenge is fitting modern MEPFS systems into old structures without damaging the historic fabric. Source: ICOMOS Principles for the Analysis, Conservation and Structural Restoration of Architectural Heritage (2003); Burra Charter (ICOMOS Australia, 2013); RA 10066 (National Cultural Heritage Act), Sec. 3.

q: Urban planners and conservation authorities often face competing pressures between upgrading built environments for contemporary needs and retaining the historical character of established districts. Achieving an effective balance requires a framework that respects both functional improvement and cultural continuity. Which statement best expresses this balanced approach?
o: Balance is achieved when modernization is allowed to reshape historic areas as long as key landmarks are retained
Balance is achieved when preservation controls are relaxed to accommodate large-scale redevelopment in strategic zones
Balance is achieved when modernization improves function and livability, while preservation protects identity, authenticity, and cultural value
Balance is achieved when new developments imitate historic styles so that old and new are visually indistinguishable
n: Balance means modernization improves function and livability while preservation protects identity, authenticity and cultural value. Source: UNESCO Recommendation on the Historic Urban Landscape (2011).

q: A heritage building along Calle Crisologo in Vigan, originally a 19th-century Bahay na Bato, was recently transformed into a boutique hotel. The intervention retained its capiz windows, thick masonry walls, and timber structural members while integrating modern plumbing, air-conditioning, fire-safety systems, and contemporary guest amenities. This project is cited by the local government as a model for how to balance heritage preservation and modernization ina UNESCO World Heritage city. Which heritage approach best describes this intervention?
n: Converting a bahay na bato into a hotel while keeping its historic fabric and adding modern services is adaptive reuse. Source: Burra Charter (ICOMOS Australia, 2013); RA 10066 (National Cultural Heritage Act), Sec. 3.

q: After decades of neglect, the Manila Metropolitan Theater (MET)—an Art Deco landmark designed by Juan M. Arellano—underwent a government-led project. The intervention involved stabilizing the original structural frame, repairing surviving Art Deco ornamentation, reinstating missing facade details based on archival drawings, and restoring interior finishes using period-accurate materials and craftsmanship. No new functions were introduced beyond its original purpose as a performance venue, and the goal was to return the building to its documented earlier state. Which type of heritage intervention best describes this project?
n: Bringing the MET back to its documented earlier state, with period-accurate repairs and no new function, is restoration. Source: Burra Charter (ICOMOS Australia, 2013); RA 10066 (National Cultural Heritage Act), Sec. 3 (restoration).

q: In a historic district of a major Visayas port city, a 19th-century commercial structure built during the Spanish colonial period was conserved and reprogrammed rather than replaced. Its original masonry walls, timber upper floors, capiz-paneled openings, and clay tile roofing were retained, while the interior was adapted to accommodate contemporary administrative functions alongside curated exhibition spaces displaying archival materials, period furnishings, and artifacts illustrating the evolution of commerce in the region. Which building best fits this description?
n: The BPI Museum in Cebu occupies BPI's historic Spanish-era commercial building. It still works as a bank office while exhibiting the history of regional commerce. Source: BPI Foundation, BPI Museum Cebu.

q: The former Old Legislative Building in Manila—originally designed by Ralph Harrington Deane and Antonio Toledo—was heavily damaged during World War H, repaired in the postwar period, and later abandoned after the Batasang Pambansa was built in Quezon City. Instead of restoring it to its former governmental function, ihe structure was repurposed by the National Museum into the National Museum of Fine Arts, housing the country's most important art collections, including the Spoliarium. The intervention preserved the building's neoclassical YET 32h architecture while giving it a completely new cultural function. Which type of heritage intervention best describes this transformation?
n: Turning the Old Legislative Building into the National Museum of Fine Arts, a new function in preserved fabric, is adaptive reuse. Source: Burra Charter (ICOMOS Australia, 2013); RA 10066 (National Cultural Heritage Act), Sec. 3; National Museum of the Philippines.

q: Before the 2023 fire, the Manila Central Post Office underwent multiple phases of work that included repairing water-damaged ceilings, replacing deteriorated interior partitions, updating lighting and electrical systerns, repainting surfaces, and improving office layouts to meet mode:.. operational needs. These intervention did not attempt to return the building to a specific historical period, nor did they introduce a new function. The goal was simply to repair, update, and improve the existing spaces so the building could continue functioning as the headquarters of the Philippine Postal Corporation. Which type cf heritage intervention best describes this work?
o: Conservation MASTERS OF ARCHITECTURE / ICONIC ST RUCTU RES
n: Repairing and updating the Post Office for its continuing use, without returning to a period or adding a function, is renovation. Source: Burra Charter (ICOMOS Australia, 2013); RA 10066 (National Cultural Heritage Act), Sec. 3.

q: Which iconic structure, originally built for the 1889 World's Fair, is celebrated as a triumph of engineering—featuring over 18,000 iron components, precise wind-load calculations, and a lattice design that demonstrated the architectural potential of exposed metal?
n: The Eiffel Tower (1889 World's Fair) used over 18,000 wrought-iron parts and precise wind-load calculations. Source: Société d'Exploitation de la Tour Eiffel; Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History.

q: Which mid-20th-century designer created the iconic Tulip Chair—characterized by its single pedestal base, molded fiberglass seat, and minimalist form—as part of a collection aimed at eliminating the "slum of legs" in furniture design?
n: Eero Saarinen designed the Tulip Chair (1957), on a single pedestal, to end the "slum of legs." Source: Knoll, Saarinen Tulip Collection.

q: Which architect founded the Bauhaus school in 1919 in Weimar, Germany—establishing a revolutionary design movement that unified art, craft, and technology, and emphasized functionalism, simplicity, and mass production?
n: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919. Source: Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History.

q: Which London skyscraper, designed by Norman Foster and commonly known as "The Gherkin," is celebrated for its aerodynamic form, energy-efficient systems, and diagrid structure—standing 180 meters tall in the heart of the city's financial district?
n: 30 St Mary Axe ("The Gherkin," Foster + Partners, 2004) is the 180 m diagrid tower in the City of London. Source: Foster + Partners project profile.

q: Which Brazilian architect, a pioneer of modernist architecture, created the Cathedral of Our Lady of Aparecida in Brasília—featuring 16 soaring concrete columns that form a hyperboloid structure symbolizing hands reaching toward heaven?
n: Oscar Niemeyer designed the Cathedral of Brasília (Our Lady of Aparecida), with 16 hyperboloid concrete columns like hands reaching to heaven. Source: Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History; IPHAN.

q: Which project marked Eero Saarinen's first major solo architectural achievement—celebrated for its pioneering use of glass curtain walls, aluminum panels, and modular steel framing, and recognized as a landmark of mid-century modernism that redefined industrial architecture?
n: The General Motors Technical Center (1956) was Eero Saarinen's first major solo work, a landmark of curtain walls and modular steel. Source: Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History.

q: Which ancient Roman structure, originally commissioned by Marcus Agrippa and rebuilt under Emperor Hadrian, is celebrated for its massive unreinforced concrete dome, central oculus, and harmonious classical proportions—making it one of the most influential and enduring architectural achievements in history?
n: The Pantheon, commissioned by Agrippa and rebuilt by Hadrian, has the great unreinforced concrete dome with its central oculus. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Roman Architecture.

q: Which iconic Byzantine structure, commissioned by Emperor Justinian and completed in 537 CE, is renowned for its fusion of basilica and centralized plan, its massive dome supported by pendentives, and its enduring legacy as a prototype for Byzantine architecture—later serving as a mosque, then a museum, and reconsecrated as a mosque in the 21st century?
o: Church of St. Sergius and Bacchus
n: Hagia Sophia (537) fuses basilica and central plan under a pendentive dome. It was later a mosque, then a museum, and in 2020 a mosque again. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Byzantine Architecture.

q: The Palm House located in the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, London specializes in growing palms and other tropical and subtropical plants, many of them endangered or extinct in the wild. It is also notable as it employed glass and the first large-scale structural use of wrought iron. Who built and designed this iconic structure?
n: The Palm House at Kew (1844–48) was designed and built by Decimus Burton and Richard Turner. It was the first large-scale structural use of wrought iron. Source: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, Palm House history.

q: Which of the following buildings marked Norman Foster's first major solo architectural commission after the dissolution of Team 4, showcasing his early commitment to transparency, open-plan design, and high-tech materials?
o: Sainsbury Centre for Visual Arts, Norwich
n: The Willis Faber & Dumas headquarters in Ipswich (1975) was Foster's first major commission after Team 4, with an open plan and frameless glass skin. Source: Foster + Partners project profile.

q: Which architect is widely regarded as the father of Tropical Modernism, known for blending modernist principles with vernacular traditions and designing buildings that harmonized with ther natural surroundings?
n: Geoffrey Bawa is regarded as the father of Tropical Modernism. Source: Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History; Robson, Geoffrey Bawa: The Complete Works.

q: Which architect, often hailed as the father of American architecture, introduced neoclassical design to the United States and is credited with major works such as the U.S. Capitol Building, the Baltimore Basilica (America's first Roman Catholic cathedral), the Bank of Pennsylvania (an early Greek Revival structure}, and the original waterworks for Philadelphia and New Orleans?
n: Benjamin Henry Latrobe, called the father of American architecture, worked on the U.S. Capitol and designed the Baltimore Basilica, the Bank of Pennsylvania and the Philadelphia and New Orleans waterworks. Source: Library of Congress, Latrobe papers.

q: The Beijing National Stadium designed by Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron is also known as
n: Herzog & de Meuron's Beijing National Stadium is known as the Bird's Nest. Source: Herzog & de Meuron project profile.

q: A 1st-century BCE Roman architect who served under Julius Caesar and Augustus. His work, De Architectura, combines the history of ancient architecture and engineering with his personal experience and advice on the subject.
n: Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (1st c. BCE), who served under Caesar and Augustus, wrote De Architectura. Source: Vitruvius, De Architectura (trans. Morgan).

q: Who is widely regarded as the first architect and engineer in recorded history?
n: Imhotep, builder of Djoser's Step Pyramid, is regarded as the first architect and engineer in recorded history. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Egyptian Architecture.

q: An American architect who pioneered the Prairie School and organic architecture movements. He designed over 1,000 structures including iconic houses like the Fallingwater and the Robie House.
n: Frank Lloyd Wright pioneered the Prairie School and organic architecture and designed Fallingwater and the Robie House. Source: Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation.

q: The main gallery of this museum contains a six-storey helical ramp that extends along its perimeter, as well as a central ceiling skylight. The museum's building is a landmark work of 20th-century architecture designed by Frank Lloyd Wright.
n: The Guggenheim Museum in New York (Wright, 1959) has a six-storey helical ramp under a central skylight. Source: Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation; Guggenheim Museum.

q: The Louvre in Abu Dhabi was designed as a seemingly floating dome structure. Its web-patterned dome allows the rays of the sun to filter through, an effect that represents sunlight passing through date palms in an oasis. Who designed this structure, which is the fruit of an agreement between the UAE and France?
n: Jean Nouvel designed the Louvre Abu Dhabi. Its latticed dome filters light like sun through date palms. Source: Ateliers Jean Nouvel; Louvre Abu Dhabi.

q: Which master architect is known for designing context-sensitive buildings such as the Institut du Monde Arabe in Paris and the Louvre Abu Dhabi—employing light-filtering facades, cultural symbolism, and innovative materials to create architecture that responds to climate, history, and place?
n: Jean Nouvel designed the Institut du Monde Arabe and the Louvre Abu Dhabi, both with light-filtering facades rooted in cultural symbolism. Source: Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

q: Which of the following buildings, known for its bold geometric form and controversial integration of modernism with historical architecture, was designed by I.M. Pei and now serves as the main entrance to a world-renowned museum in Paris?
n: I.M. Pei's Louvre Pyramid (1989) is the main entrance of the Louvre in Paris. Source: Pei Cobb Freed & Partners; Musée du Louvre.

q: Which early 20th-century Parisian building, designed by Auguste Perret, is recognized as the first major structure in the city built entirely of reinforced concrete—featuring a coffered ceiling that allows natural light to penetrate the auditorium, a facade with classical proportions and geometric ornamentation, and a design that helped usher in the modernist movement in architecture?
n: Auguste Perret's Théâtre des Champs-Élysées (1913) was the first major Paris building entirely in reinforced concrete. Source: Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History.

q: Buckminster Fuller is an American architect and inventor who popularized, is widely credited with, and patented (in the US) the use of:
n: Buckminster Fuller popularized and patented (US, 1954) the geodesic dome. Walther Bauersfeld's Zeiss planetarium dome came earlier. Source: Buckminster Fuller Institute.

q: In the 1960s, during the height of the space race and the burgeoning of space travel, Buckminster Fuller proposed the creation of
n: Fuller proposed "Cloud Nine," floating airborne cities in huge geodesic spheres. Source: Buckminster Fuller Institute (Cloud Nine, c. 1960).

q: Which visionary architect and inventor designed the US pavilion at expo 67 in Montreal?
n: Buckminster Fuller designed the US Pavilion at Expo 67 in Montreal, a 76 m geodesic dome (now the Biosphère). Source: Buckminster Fuller Institute.

q: The Center Pompidou-Metz is a museum of modern and contemporary art located in Metz, France. The building is remarkable for its roof structure which was inspired by a Chinese hat. Which architect designed this structure?
n: Shigeru Ban designed the Centre Pompidou-Metz, whose timber roof was inspired by a Chinese hat. Source: Shigeru Ban Architects; Centre Pompidou-Metz.

q: His works introduced a new level-of simplicity and transparency, and his buildings were often referred to as "skin-and-bones" architecture for their emphasis on steel structure and glass enclosure.
n: Mies van der Rohe's steel-and-glass buildings were called "skin-and-bones" architecture. Source: Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History.

q: The Robie House is a US National Historic Landmark in the campus of the University of Chicago. Who is its Architect?
n: The Robie House (1910) at the University of Chicago is by Frank Lloyd Wright. Source: Frank Lloyd Wright Trust.

q: A masterpiece of simplicity and clarity showcasing the architect's philosophy of "less is more," this is the celebrated glass house designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe in Plano, Illinois.
n: The Farnsworth House (1951) shows Mies's "less is more" in a single glass room lifted on steel. Source: Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History; National Trust for Historic Preservation.

q: The Portland Building in Oregon, designed by Michael Graves and completed in 1982, is widely recognized as an iconic example of which architectural style?
n: Michael Graves's Portland Building (1982) is an icon of Postmodernism. Source: Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History.

q: The National Museum of Western Art located in Ueno Park, Taito, Tokyo is the premier public art gallery in Japan specializing in Western traditional art. Who designed the main building?
n: Le Corbusier designed the main building of the National Museum of Western Art in Tokyo (1959), now a UNESCO site. Source: UNESCO, The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier.

q: The Japan National Stadium in Shinjuku, Tokyo was the main stadium used for the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2020 Summer Olympics. Who is its architect?
n: Kengo Kuma designed the Japan National Stadium for the Tokyo 2020 Olympics. Source: Kengo Kuma & Associates; Japan Sport Council.

q: The Imperial War Museum North was based on the concept of a globe scattered by conflict into shards and reassembled. These shards representing earth, air and water, give the building its shape. It is located in Manchester. Who designed this building?
n: Daniel Libeskind designed the Imperial War Museum North, a globe shattered into shards of earth, air and water. Source: Studio Libeskind.

q: The Hiroshima Peace Center and Memorial Park expressed the solidarity of human kind as well as symbolizing a commitment to peace. It is a work of
n: Kenzo Tange designed the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park and Museum. Source: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum; Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History.
